q: What is the top tier of the Saint-Emilion classification?
exp: Below it sit Premier Grand Cru Classe B and then Grand Cru Classe. Note that plain Saint-Emilion Grand Cru is an appellation, not a rank.

q: The Saint-Emilion classification differs from the 1855 in one fundamental way. Which?
opts: It was created by Napoleon III
exp: The 1855 list has changed once in more than a century and a half. Saint-Emilion rebuilds its ranking periodically, with all the argument that invites.

q: Which two chateaux were the original Premier Grand Cru Classe A?
exp: Ausone and Cheval Blanc held the top rank alone for decades before the category was widened, and the membership has moved since.

q: Sauternes owes its sweetness chiefly to what?
opts: Freezing the fruit on the vine
exp: Botrytis cinerea pierces the skin and the berry dehydrates, concentrating sugar and acid and adding its own honeyed character.

q: The cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne each autumn. Why does that matter?
exp: Mist forms overnight and burns off in afternoon sun. That damp-then-dry alternation is exactly what noble rot needs and grey rot does not get.

q: One commune inside the Sauternes area may use its own appellation. Which?
exp: Barsac wines may be labelled either Barsac or Sauternes. Barsac sits on more limestone and is often a shade lighter in style.

q: Yields in Sauternes are famously low. What drives that?
opts: The berries shrivel to little juice
Only one press cycle is permitted
exp: A shrivelled berry yields little juice, and pickers take only what is ready. Yquem's output per vine is proverbially close to a single glass.

q: Across the Garonne from Sauternes lies which sweet white appellation?
exp: Loupiac, Cadillac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont face Sauternes from the opposite bank and make botrytis-affected sweet whites at gentler prices.

q: Pickers in Sauternes pass through the vineyard repeatedly through the harvest. What is that practice called?
exp: Successive passes take only the berries that have reached the right state of botrytis. It is slow, weather-dependent and the main reason for the cost.

q: Age-worthy dry white Bordeaux is most associated with which appellation?
exp: Barrel-fermented Sauvignon and Semillon from Pessac-Leognan are the region's serious whites, and the best age for decades.

q: The Entre-Deux-Mers appellation may be used for which style?
exp: The appellation covers dry white wine. Red wine grown in the same area is sold as Bordeaux or Bordeaux Superieur instead.

q: Semillon is blended with Sauvignon Blanc for what reason?
opts: It adds the aroma that Sauvignon Blanc lacks
exp: The pairing is complementary: Semillon's broad, waxy palate fills out Sauvignon's sharper aromatic drive, and it also ages well.

q: Barrel fermentation contributes what to a white Pessac-Leognan?
exp: Fermenting and ageing in barrel builds body and integrates oak more gently than ageing alone, and lees work adds further texture.

q: A third grape adds a floral, grapey lift in small amounts to white Bordeaux. Which?
exp: Muscadelle is used in small proportions for perfume. It is unrelated to the Muscat family despite the resemblance in name.

q: What structural feature defines a red Bordeaux?
opts: It is typically a blend of permitted varieties
It is aged only in stainless steel, never oak
It is fortified with spirit after fermentation
It is always a single variety, never blended
exp: Blending is the region's central idea: the permitted varieties ripen differently and hedge each other across vintages, and the assemblage is decided each year. A handful of estates end up close to monovarietal.

q: Buying a wine as futures, before it is bottled, is known as what?
exp: Wine is offered in the spring after harvest while still in barrel, and delivered a couple of years later. It funds the chateau and sets the vintage's price.
